newsitem.title: ESTONIA: ANALYSIS - ESTONIAN INSURERS OPTIMISTIC ON LIFE MARKET.
newsitem.headline: ANALYSIS - ESTONIAN INSURERS OPTIMISTIC ON LIFE MARKET.

text.p: Following a boom in Estonia's banking market, analysts said on Friday that the life insurance market was the financial sector that is next set for rapid growth if it gets support on the legislative side.
Non-life business has traditionally been the most active in Estonia but analysts said the room for most growth was in life.
"There could be a boom if some tax allowances are made," Hansapank Insurance chairman Mart Einpalu said.
"The increase depends on the insurance companies mostly, on their abilities to catch customers and sell a good image," Einpalu told Reuters.

Finnish firms have also become interested in the market of their Estonian neighbour, just 80 kms across the Gulf of Finland, and Pohjola recently bought a stake in life insurer Seesam-Elu with Estonian bank Uhispank.

Estonian insurance companies say one of the impeding factors to the growth of the life market is that pension reform has not yet been implemented and that income tax is charged on life insurance payments, which companies hope to be changed.
Einpalu added that people are also expecting an end to the stock market boom, which has seen share prices rocket, and were looking for more stable investment oppurtunities.
Estonia's life-insurance market was 65 million kroons in 1996 and is estimated to grow to 100 million kroons this year.
Insurance companies collected 840 million kroons in premiums last year, which is up from 1995 by 52 percent. Most premiums came from traffic insurance: 335 million kroons.
Eesti Kindlustus (Estonian Insurance) sales group director Eduard Saul said the life market was disproportionately small, as it made up only under 10 percent of the total market.
"An explosive increase may be possible after some political decisions are taken," he said.
He said that total insurance premiums collected were estimated to reach one billion kroons at the end of this year and that his company expected to have a quarter of the market.
Heido Vitsur, an advisor to the prime minister on economic affairs, said that further growth in the life-insurance market depended on people's earnings and slowing inflation.
"As earnings are on the increase and inflation on the decrease, life insurance may become interesting," Vitsur said.
Non-life insurance is also estimated to grow, as companies have started to think about avoiding risks, Vitsur said.
Further growth in the compulsory traffic insurance, which has the biggest or almost 40 percent of the total market, depends on new car sales, Vitsur said.
"The growth in car sales is however limited," he added.
Travel insurance will also grow in line with tourism, Vitsur added.
Saul from Kindlustus said the insurance market will restructure over the following years as 14 non-life and 16 life-insurance companies were too much for Estonia.
Saul also noted there were a number of insurance companies seeking a listing on the stock exchange.
Insurer Leks hopes to get a listing on the bourse this year and Eesti Kindlustus in about a year.
